relevance: The left and right cardiac border extremes and the inner thoracic width define the cardiothoracic ratio, the standard radiographic index of cardiomegaly (CTR > 0.5 on PA films).

Blunting of the costophrenic angles (lateral on the frontal view, posterior and anterior on the lateral view) is the earliest radiographic sign of pleural effusion, and the angles are mandated image-quality criteria.
The cardiophrenic angles are where pericardial fat pads, pericardial cysts, Morgagni hernias and enlarged paracardiac nodes appear as masses obscuring the angle.
The height of the diaphragm dome and flattening of its contour are the main radiographic markers of inspiratory effort and of hyperinflation or emphysema.
The lung apex relative to the cupola, and the lateral lung margin relative to the chest wall, are the landmarks used to estimate pneumothorax size and guide management.
The position of the hila (the left normally higher than the right) and their relative height detect volume loss, lobar collapse and hilar masses.

Mediastinal lines and stripes (right paratracheal stripe, paraspinal lines, para-aortic line) are air-tissue interfaces whose displacement or thickening reveals mediastinal masses, adenopathy, hematoma or effusion.
Mediastinal width and the contours of its borders screen for mediastinal hemorrhage and traumatic aortic injury (widening above about 8 cm) and for mediastinal masses.
The width and calcification of the aortic knob (arch summit) are radiographic markers of aortic dilatation or unfolding and of atherosclerosis or arterial stiffness.
Convexity or obliteration of the aortopulmonary window (the concave interface between the aortic arch and the pulmonary trunk) is a classic sign of mediastinal adenopathy or a mass.
The width of the pulmonary trunk and of the right descending pulmonary artery, together with hilar artery enlargement, are radiographic indicators of pulmonary hypertension.

The carina, the main bronchi and the tracheal bifurcation (carinal) angle mark tracheal position and are the ETT-tip reference; widening of the angle is a classic sign of left atrial enlargement or subcarinal mass.

Displacement of the trachea from the midline between inlet and carina is a classic CXR sign of mass effect (tension pneumothorax, goitre, large effusion) or of volume loss pulling toward the abnormal side.

The carina is the radiographic reference for endotracheal-tube tip depth and a surrogate for the cavoatrial junction, which is the target for a central venous catheter tip, so both are checked on almost every ICU CXR.

After nasogastric tube insertion, the CXR must show the tube following the oesophagus in the midline, bisecting the carina, crossing the diaphragm and ending below the left hemidiaphragm in the gastric air bubble; a misplaced tube in the airway is a never event.
The right atrial border, left atrial appendage bulge, double-density sign, carinal splaying and LV apex position are the classic frontal-CXR signs of individual cardiac chamber enlargement.

The jugular notch, sternal angle and xiphoid are surface and radiographic reference levels: the sternal angle is classically taught at T4/5 and the carina, and these are used for mediastinal levels and device positioning.

The medial clavicle ends relative to the spinous processes are the standard check for patient rotation, and the scapulae must be projected outside the lung fields on a technically adequate PA chest film.

Vertebral endplate corners define the Cobb angle for scoliosis on the frontal view and the anterior/middle/posterior heights used to grade wedge or compression fractures on the lateral CXR, where incidental fractures are often under-reported.
Counting posterior and anterior ribs above the diaphragm is the standard check of inspiratory adequacy, and the rib ends and costal junctions locate rib fractures.

Radiographic severity scores divide each lung into fixed zones or quadrants (RALE: quadrants; Brixia: six zones defined by the aortic arch and inferior pulmonary hila), so zone landmarks directly drive scoring.
The position and shape of the interlobar fissures, especially displacement of the minor fissure, are the direct signs of lobar volume loss and collapse on the CXR.
Nipple and breast shadows are common nodule mimics in the lower zones, so locating them prevents false-positive nodule calls and unnecessary work-up.
Scapulae must be projected outside the lung fields on a technically adequate PA chest film; together with rotation (clavicles) and inspiration (ribs) they set the technical-quality rating.
